title: Divide Chocolate
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every cut combination versus binary search on the minimum-sweetness threshold, using a greedy achievable-piece-count as the feasibility check.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: You have a chocolate bar made of contiguous chunks, sweetness[i] being the sweetness of chunk i. You will cut the bar into k+1 contiguous pieces to share with k friends (keeping one piece for yourself), each piece's sweetness being the sum of its chunks. Maximize the MINIMUM total sweetness of the piece you eat (you always take the piece with the least total sweetness, so maximizing that value maximizes what you are guaranteed to get).

blocks.text: As the required minimum sweetness per piece increases, the number of pieces that can be carved out while meeting that minimum can only decrease or stay the same. This is the "maximize the minimum" mirror image of Split Array Largest Sum's "minimize the maximum," using the same binary-search-on-the-answer technique.

blocks.title: Analogy: Cutting a Long Cake to Guarantee Everyone a Decent-Sized Slice
blocks.text: Picture cutting a long, unevenly-iced cake into a fixed number of pieces so that even the SMALLEST piece still has a good amount of icing. Requiring more icing per piece means fewer pieces can meet that bar; binary searching over the required icing amount finds the highest bar still achievable with the needed number of pieces.

blocks.caption: A higher required minimum sweetness always allows fewer or equal achievable pieces, enabling binary search

blocks.text: Result: 6. Splitting into 6 pieces (k+1=6) such as [1,2,3],[4,5],[6],[7],[8],[9] gives piece sums 6,9,6,7,8,9; the minimum among these is 6, the best achievable.

Before trying every possible way to cut the bar into k+1 pieces, notice that the number of pieces achievable while requiring each to have at least a candidate sweetness threshold is a monotonically non-increasing function of that threshold, letting binary search directly find the maximum feasible threshold.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed candidate threshold, a GREEDY left-to-right scan (accumulate chunks into the current piece; once its sum reaches the threshold, "cut" it off and start a new piece) computes the MAXIMUM number of pieces achievable while keeping every piece at least that sweet.

Observation 2: The minimum possible threshold is min(sweetness) (a single chunk alone), and the maximum useful threshold is sum(sweetness) divided by (k+1) (the average, an upper bound on the achievable minimum).

Observation 3: As the candidate threshold increases within this range, the greedy achievable piece count can only decrease or stay the same, a monotonic relationship.

Observation 4: Binary searching over this range, checking whether the greedy piece count is at least k+1 (searching for a possibly higher threshold if so, lower if not), converges on the maximum achievable threshold.

This leads to binary searching over candidate minimum-sweetness thresholds, computing the greedy achievable piece count at each candidate, and narrowing toward the maximum threshold for which at least k+1 pieces are achievable.
Try every way to cut the bar into exactly k+1 contiguous pieces (via recursion choosing cut points), tracking the maximum possible minimum piece sweetness across all valid cuts.

items: Recursively try every position to place the next cut, given a remaining number of pieces to form.
For each complete split into exactly k+1 pieces, compute the minimum piece sweetness.
Track and return the maximum such minimum sweetness across all valid splits.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every possible cut combination directly implements the definition, guaranteed correct.
This explores an exponential number of ways to place k cuts among n-1 possible positions, far too slow beyond small inputs.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case.
Space: O(n) recursion depth plus O(n) for prefix sums.

Limitation: since the achievable piece count for a given threshold is monotonic, binary search on the candidate threshold, using a greedy piece-count check, achieves O(n log(sum(sweetness))) instead of exploring every cut combination.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every cut combination is unnecessary: the actual GOAL is just to find the maximum feasible threshold, and a greedy piece-count check at a fixed threshold can be computed directly in O(n), without trying every cut position.

The binary search reformulation: binary search over candidate thresholds in [min(sweetness), sum(sweetness)/(k+1)]; for each candidate, greedily determine the maximum number of pieces achievable while keeping every piece at least that sweet.

Why the greedy check is valid: for a FIXED threshold, greedily cutting off a piece as SOON as its accumulated sum reaches the threshold (rather than waiting) always achieves the maximum possible number of pieces for that threshold.

The core idea: binary search directly on the answer (the threshold), using an O(n) greedy piece-count as the monotonic feasibility check, searching for the LARGEST feasible threshold this time (the mirror image of Split Array's smallest feasible cap).

Binary search threshold in [min(sweetness), sum(sweetness)/(k+1)]. At each step, greedily count pieces achievable at that threshold (cutting off a piece as soon as its sum reaches the threshold); if pieces achievable >= k+1, the threshold is feasible (search for a possibly higher threshold); otherwise search lower.

blocks.caption: Binary search the threshold, using a greedy achievable-piece-count as the feasibility check

blocks.text: The greedy achievable-piece-count function is optimal for a fixed threshold: cutting off a piece the moment its accumulated sum reaches the threshold never wastes potential sweetness that could have started a new piece sooner, maximizing the total pieces formed. Since this achievable count is monotonically non-increasing in the threshold, the binary search (biased to find the MAXIMUM feasible value this time) correctly converges: feasible thresholds (achievable pieces >= k+1) allow trying an even higher threshold, while infeasible ones require trying lower, converging exactly on the maximum achievable minimum piece sweetness.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "maximize the minimum piece when splitting into exactly k+1 contiguous groups", think: binary search on the threshold (searching for the LARGEST feasible value), using a greedy achievable-piece-count as the feasibility check.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The exponential cut-combination search is infeasible beyond small inputs; binary search with a greedy feasibility check runs in O(n times log(sum(sweetness))) time and O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer (the minimum piece threshold), using a greedy achievable-piece-count as the monotonic feasibility check, searching for the MAXIMUM feasible value.
Core Idea: binary search the threshold; greedily count pieces achievable (cut off as soon as a piece qualifies); narrow toward the maximum threshold with at least k+1 achievable pieces.
Time: exponential for trying every cut, O(n times log(sum(sweetness))) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: this is the "maximize the minimum" dual of Split Array Largest Sum's "minimize the maximum," using the same technique with the search direction reversed.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known variant testing whether the binary-search-on-the-answer technique is understood deeply enough to apply in reverse.
One line memory trick: binary search the threshold (search for the max feasible); greedily count achievable pieces as the check.
